context: Several tickets, all at the same price, are bought for one total amount in rand (R). The price of a single ticket must be found and given to the nearest cent, that is, rounded to 2 decimal places.
stem: If ${=n}$ tickets cost $\text{R}{=tot}$ , how much does one ticket cost? Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
solution: One ticket costs the total cost divided by the number of tickets: $\text{R}{=tot}\div{=n}$ .

Money is rounded off to $2$ decimal places (the nearest cent). The digits up to the second decimal place are ${=keep}$ and the next digit is ${=d}$ . A digit of $5$ or more rounds the last kept digit up by $1$ ; a smaller digit leaves it as it is.
Therefore one ticket costs $\text{R}{=ans}$ , correct to $2$ decimal places.
notes: Entry point of the objective: one division, then one rounding to a stated number of decimal places. Skeleton and context are the book's ex1-2-6 (tickets, the Rand, money rounded to 2 decimal places); the stem states the 2 decimal places so that the instance is not ambiguous for a first exposure. Parameters: n tickets in {3, 6, 7, 9, 11} and a total of R15.00 to R99.99 held as whole cents c. The constraint (2c) % n != 0 guarantees that every instance really needs rounding (the price is never already a whole number of cents) and never sits exactly halfway between two cents (so no round-half-up versus round-half-even disagreement). With these n the quotient is always a non-terminating decimal, so the '...' in step 2 is always true; the displayed value is the quotient TRUNCATED to 5 decimal places, never rounded, so it cannot disagree with the final rounding. Step 3 is deliberately worded to be true for any digit (no 'round up' / 'stays' branch), so every instance's steps are true. The answer is printed with 2 decimals, trailing zero kept (as the book prints R14.80). Checked offline against Decimal ROUND_HALF_UP for 20 000 draws: answers range R1.36 to R33.33. No distractors: numeric answer, so no misconception ids are attached.
